In August, the AVROTROS broadcaster, which selects the Dutch entry and broadcasts the show, had pulled out. NPO replaced it only to reverse its decision on October 27, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

The Netherlands will not participate in next year's Eurovision Song Contest, its public broadcaster NPO said on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation.

The Dutch withdrawal is the latest in a series of boycotts from countries unhappy at Israel's inclusion in the annual music festival, given its military campaign in Gaza sparked by the October 7 Hamas attacks.

"We have known for some time that Israel's participation elicits various reactions in society and causes discussion and division," said Jurre Bosman, NPO's media director, in a statement.

"Therefore, after consultation with the Board of Broadcasters, the NPO has decided to forgo participation in 2027," added Mr. Bosman.

The Dutch decision brings to an end a series of flip-flops over its participation, highlighting the divisive nature of the debate in the country and more broadly.

In August, the AVROTROS broadcaster, which selects the Dutch entry and broadcasts the show, had pulled out, saying the event can "no longer be considered neutral" given divisions over the Gaza war.

But a month later, NPO stepped in to replace AVROTROS, saying it would take on the responsibility, only to reverse course with its decision on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).

Jet de Ranitz, NPO's executive chairman, acknowledged their decision would disappoint many Dutch Eurovision fans and stressed that the contest would still be aired on the public channels.

However, he said, "We must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027."

"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being," added Mr. De Ranitz.

In August, organisers announced they were excluding any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.

But that has not prevented withdrawals, with Ireland already announcing they would not take part and the head of the Spanish public broadcaster also coming out in favour of a boycott.

Earlier this month, the Czech public broadcaster pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.

Next year's contest, the world's biggest live televised music event, will take place on May 15 in Bulgaria's Black Sea city of Burgas.

It will be the first time the Balkan nation has hosted the contest, coming after Bulgarian singer Darina Yotova, known as Dara, won this year's contest in the Austrian capital Vienna with the catchy floor-filler "Bangaranga".

Since its launch in 1955, Eurovision has become the ultimate pop platform, catapulting Swedish icons ABBA to worldwide fame, as well as boosting the likes of Celine Dion, Cliff Richard and Olivia Newton-John.

The 2026 competition was watched by 131 million viewers, down 35 million on the year before after five countries boycotted it over Israel's participation.

The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the 2026 contest, with the latter three refusing to broadcast the show at all.

The Dutch took part in the very first Eurovision Song Contest back in 1956, and have won on five occasions.

Their most recent winner was Duncan Laurence, whose song Arcade won the contest in 2019, going on to top charts globally.

It became the first Eurovision entry to reach one billion streams on Spotify, according to the Eurovision website.

The head of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU), which organises the show, said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not be taking part.

"We understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it in the Netherlands," said Martin Green in a statement.

"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world."

#865. Iran: Mehr Druck auf Frauen ohne Hidschab

Immer mehr Frauen in der Islamischen Republik widersetzen sich der Hidschab-Pflicht. Hardliner setzen zunehmend auf sozialen Druck - statt auf die "Sittenpolizei" auf der Straße.

Frauen, die in der Öffentlichkeit ohne Hidschab unterwegs sind, gehören inzwischen in vielen Teilen Irans zum alltäglichen Straßenbild. Es ist eine der sichtbarsten gesellschaftlichen Veränderungen seit den Protesten der Bewegung "Frau, Leben, Freiheit" im Jahr 2022. Ausgelöst wurden diese nach dem Tod der jungen Frau Jina Mahsa Amini in Polizeigewahrsam, die wegen eines angeblich nicht korrekt getragenen Kopftuchs festgenommen worden war.

Den Behörden ist es bislang nicht gelungen, das Ausmaß an Straßenkontrollen aus der Zeit vor den Protesten wiederherzustellen. Der teilweise Rückzug der berüchtigten "Sittenpolizei" bedeutet jedoch nicht, dass sie die Durchsetzung der Hidschab-Pflicht für Frauen aufgegeben haben.

Behörden und konservative Kreise suchen nach neuen Wegen, den gesellschaftlichen Wandel einzudämmen, ohne die offenen Konfrontationen auf der Straße wiederzubeleben, die 2022 maßgeblich zu den Protesten beigetragen hatten. Justizchef Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei forderte kürzlich ein härteres Vorgehen gegen das, was er als gesellschaftliche "Abweichungen", "Unsittlichkeit" und "Nacktheit" bezeichnete. Staatsanwälte sollten dabei enger mit Polizei, Geheimdiensten und staatlichen Institutionen zusammenarbeiten.

Gleichzeitig werben Unterstützer der Hidschab-Pflicht in Online-Kampagnen dafür, Geschäfte von Frauen zu meiden, die sich nicht an die staatlichen Kleidervorschriften halten. Stattdessen sollen Kundinnen und Kunden gezielt bei Frauen einkaufen, die den Hidschab tragen. Die Folge ist eine stärker zersplitterte Form der Kontrolle, die sich zunehmend von Polizeipatrouillen hin zu Arbeitsplätzen, Unternehmen und alltäglichen Dienstleistungen verlagert.

Die Initiatoren der Online-Kampagnen sprechen von "bewusstem Konsum" und rufen dazu auf, gezielt Anbieterinnen zu unterstützen, die den Hidschab tragen. Eine Anwältin aus Teheran erklärt gegenüber der DW unter der Bedingung der Anonymität, solche Kampagnen könnten gesellschaftliche Spaltungen vertiefen, statt die Einhaltung gesellschaftlicher Normen zu fördern. "Dies ist ein gezielter Versuch, Menschen über ihre Identität zu kategorisieren und gegeneinander auszuspielen", sagt sie.

Wirtschaftlichen Druck allein aufgrund des äußeren Erscheinungsbildes auszuüben, gehe über das Recht des Einzelnen hinaus, frei zu entscheiden, wo er einkaufen wolle. "Wenn gegen es selbst (das Regime) Sanktionen verhängt werden, spricht das Regime von Druck, Ungerechtigkeit und Wirtschaftskrieg", sagte die Juristin. "Wenn dieselbe Logik jedoch im eigenen Land angewendet wird, um einen Teil der Gesellschaft zu einem bestimmten Verhalten zu zwingen, heißt es plötzlich: Unterstützung von Werten".

Zugleich stellt sie die Annahme infrage, dass Frauen, die sich an einen bestimmten Dresscode halten, automatisch die gesellschaftlichen Werte Irans verkörpern: "Die iranische Gesellschaft ist wesentlich komplexer als das."

Berichte iranischer Frauen in sozialen Medien deuten darauf hin, dass die Kontrolle von Kleidungsvorschriften mittlerweile auch bei Alltagsdienstleistungen eine Rolle spielt. Einige Frauen sagen, ihnen sei wegen fehlenden Kopftuchs der Zugang zu Kliniken oder Banken verweigert worden.

Shirin Shams, iranische Exilaktivistin und Leiterin der Organisation Women's Revolution Organization, sieht in den aktuellen Kampagnen den Versuch, gesellschaftliche Gräben wiederherzustellen, die während der Bewegung "Frau, Leben, Freiheit" überwunden worden seien.

"Die Islamische Republik versucht seit Jahren, Frauen anhand ihrer Kleidung gegeneinander auszuspielen", sagt die in Deutschland lebende Aktivistin der DW. Für sie stellt die Hidschab-Pflicht eine der wichtigsten ideologischen Grenzlinien des iranischen Staates dar. Die große Zahl von Frauen, die inzwischen ohne Kopftuch in der Öffentlichkeit erscheinen, zeige jedoch, wie weit sich die gesellschaftliche Realität von den offiziellen Vorstellungen entfernt habe.

Die aktuellen Kampagnen seien deshalb weit mehr als eine Debatte über Kleidung. Es gehe darum, die Trennlinie zwischen Frauen, die sich den Vorgaben fügen, und jenen, die dies nicht tun, erneut zu etablieren.

Auch der in Frankreich lehrende Soziologe Saeed Paivandi sieht darin einen grundlegenden Konflikt um gesellschaftliche Kontrolle. Der Professor der Universität Lothringen erklärt gegenüber der DW, die Behörden hätten über Jahre hinweg zwischen "korrekt verschleierten" und "schlecht verschleierten" beziehungsweise unverschleierten Frauen unterschieden. "Die Regierung macht den Körper von Frauen erneut zu einer sozialen, moralischen und sogar sicherheitspolitischen Frage", sagte Paivandi.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Eine Frau ohne Kopftuch werde nicht lediglich als jemand wahrgenommen, der eine individuelle Entscheidung trifft. Teile des politischen Establishments betrachteten sie vielmehr als sichtbare Herausforderung für die ideologische Ordnung des Staates.

Während Präsident Massud Peseschkian wiederholt die Bedeutung gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalts und nationaler Einheit betont hat, fordern konservative Richter und Politiker weiterhin eine strengere Durchsetzung der Kleidervorschriften. Dadurch entsteht ein Spannungsfeld innerhalb des iranischen Machtapparats. Ein Teil des Establishments scheint sich bewusst zu sein, dass eine Rückkehr zu großflächigen Konfrontationen zwischen Polizei und Frauen erhebliche gesellschaftliche und politische Kosten verursachen könnte.

Andere wiederum wollen die zunehmende Normalisierung des Auftretens von Frauen ohne Hidschab nicht akzeptieren. Das Ergebnis ist weder eine Rückkehr zum früheren System flächendeckender Straßenkontrollen noch das Ende der verpflichtenden Kleidervorschriften. Stattdessen zeigt sich der Druck punktuell und auf unterschiedlichen Ebenen: vor Gerichten, am Arbeitsplatz, in Unternehmen, bei Behördengängen oder durch gesellschaftliche Kampagnen.

Nach Ansicht Paivandis hat die direkte staatliche Repression ihre Grenzen erreicht. Deshalb suchten Befürworter der islamischen Kleidervorschriften nach alternativen Möglichkeiten, gesellschaftliche Konformität durchzusetzen. Dadurch werde ein Teil der Verantwortung von staatlichen Institutionen auf die Gesellschaft selbst verlagert.

Bankangestellte, Klinikmitarbeiterinnen, Arbeitgeber, Geschäftsinhaber oder Kunden könnten so zu Akteuren der Kontrolle werden, selbst wenn kein Polizist anwesend sei. Die Grenze zwischen Gesetz, persönlichem Ermessen und ideologischem Druck verschwimme dadurch zunehmend.

Zugleich warnt Paivandi, dass die Verbindung von Religion mit Ausgrenzung, Erniedrigung und Zwang besonders junge Iranerinnen und Iraner weiter von religiösen Institutionen entfremden könnte. Auch Frauen, die sich freiwillig für das Tragen eines Hidschabs entscheiden, könnten in einen Konflikt hineingezogen werden, den sie selbst nicht gewählt haben, wenn ihre Kleidung zunehmend als Zeichen politischer Loyalität interpretiert werde.

Dieser Beitrag wurde aus dem Englischen adaptiert.

#870. Serbia: Tens of thousands rally ahead of elections

After two years of student-led protests, Serbia will soon vote in what observers describe as a referendum-like snap election pitting strongman Aleksandar Vucic against the student movement.

Over a hundred thousand of Serbians took to the streets in support of Serbia's protesting youth movement on Thursday, in what was the final campaign rally ahead of a pivotal election challenge to the Balkan nation's populist strongman, Aleksandar Vucic.

Crowds poured into Belgrade's central square from all directions and filled up several blocks around the area. Independent crowd-monitoring group Archive of Public Gatherings estimated about 150,000 people were at the rally.

The optimistic crowds chanted "victory" ahead of Sunday's crunch vote which comes after two years of student-led protests against Vucic. It was triggered by a 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station which killed 16 people.

The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, has since snowballed from demands for an independent investigation into the incident, into calls for early elections.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, is the veteran leader's biggest threat.

Thousands supporting it flocked to Belgrade's streets on Thursday.

"I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country," 47-year-old Marija Nedeljkovic Radic told the French AFP news agency as she arrived for the students' rally.

"Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible," she said.

"We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours," university professor Jugoslav Gasic, one of 250 candidates on the Student List, told the crowd who chanted "Victory, victory!"

"You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!"

Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade now, either as prime minister or president of the Balkan country.

As pressure from the protests mounted, he announced a snap election last month. He has resigned as president, but many argue it is a tactical move so that he could run for prime minister.

This is now the biggest electoral challenge his party, the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), has faced since it was elected into power in 2012.

The leader, meanwhile, has regularly accused the students movement of being a foreign-funded coup.

"Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it," Vucic said to a sports hall full of supporters on Thursday. "Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!"

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Days before the vote, Serbian civil societies warned that conditions for "free and fair election" were lacking.

"This assessment is not based on isolated incidents, opposition claims or political disagreement with the government," a joint statement by 24 organisations said, arguing it was supported by documented findings.

Analysts warn that a close election result could lead to post-election instability, if both sides declare victory. Vucic, who controls the Serbian police, has said he would quash any unrest after the vote.

While several minor parties are also in the race for premiership, observers say that there is a referendum-like atmosphere between Vucic and the students' movement which could sideline other parties in the 250-member parliament.

#872. “Caminar entre tumbas es como asistir a una lección de historia del arte”: las visitas a cementerios pierden el estigma de lo siniestro

En su nuevo libro, el periodista de viajes Galo Martín ensalza el necroturismo como actividad cultural y reivindica la labor de difusión del patrimonio llevada a cabo desde los camposantos españoles

Todo el que viaja a Egipto, Roma, Praga o París, visita las pirámides, las catacumbas, el antiguo cementerio judío o el del Père Lachaise. A los arquitectos se nos cae la baba con el cementerio del Bosque de Estocolmo (1916–1940) de Gunnar Asplund y Sigurd Lewerentz, con el de San Cataldo de Módena (1971–1978) de Aldo Rossi, o con el de Igualada (1985–1996) de Enric Miralles y Carme Pinós. “La gran mayoría de los cementerios son espacios abiertos al público, tanto los municipales como los sacramentales, gratuitos, bonitos, tranquilos y llenos de historias y curiosidades”, explica el periodista especializado en viajes Galo Martín, quien lleva años haciendo necroturismo por todo el mundo. “Son lugares de encuentro donde confluyen la paz, el arte, la historia y la memoria colectiva”.

La Asociación de Cementerios Significativos de Europa (ASCE) aglutina un selecto grupo de alrededor de doscientos de estos “museos al aire libre”, tal como los define Martín. Un rápido vistazo al mapa de la web evidencia que, para sorpresa de nadie, Londres, París y Berlín son las ciudades con una mayor concentración de necrópolis inolvidables. El ranking por países, sin embargo, arroja resultados menos previsibles: con un total de 32 cementerios con encanto, el primer puesto le corresponde a España.

En su último libro, Cementerios de España (Anaya Touring, 2026), Martín emprende un bello viaje por la tanatofilia patria. Recorre desde el cementerio más pequeño de nuestro país, situado en las afueras del pueblo de Bausen, en el Vall d’Aran (provincia de Lleida), que “sólo tiene una tumba y cuenta una historia triste de amor que refleja una época que algunos parecen querer revivir”, hasta el más grande, el madrileño cementerio de la Almudena. “Tiene 120 hectáreas y entre sus muros se han enterrado a unos cinco millones de personas desde 1884”. Más allá de su tamaño, al periodista le impresiona su rico repertorio estilístico. “Hay de todo: neogótico, neorrománico, neomudéjar, modernismo y eclecticismo. Caminar entre sus mausoleos, panteones, criptas, capillas, nichos y esculturas es como asistir a una lección de historia del arte”.

Algunos de los cementerios favoritos de Martín son de autor. Es el caso del proyectado a finales del siglo XIX por el arquitecto modernista Lluís Doménech i Montaner en la pequeña localidad cántabra de Comillas, entonces un centro de experimentación arquitectónica en donde dio sus primeros pasos un jovencísimo Antoni Gaudí. Más reciente es el cementerio civil de Fisterra (1997–1999), obra del reconocido arquitecto César Portela. “En Galicia los cementerios son un derroche de galleguismo”, comenta Martín. Ubicado en lo alto de un cabo de la Costa da Morte, sus senderos discurren sobre un acantilado con vistas al Atlántico, “un proveedor de vida y muerte de Galicia”.

“Los cementerios con vistas al mar son fotogénicos y dramáticos”, explica Martín. “En Cantabria, en Galicia, en Asturias, la localización de los cementerios parece que la ha escogido un director de fotografía de una película”. ¿Alguno en particular? “Hay muchísimos, pero a mí siempre me ha llamado la atención el Panteón del Inglés que hay en Cueto, a las afueras de Santander, justo al lado de unos acantilados donde ruge el mar Cantábrico. No es un cementerio como tal, sino un discreto monumento que honra a una persona que perdió la vida al caerse de un caballo en ese lugar concreto. Me parece un sitio con una carga poética insuperable”.

El periodista también destaca el cementerio de Luarca, “un balcón desde el que contemplar el mar”, y el pequeño cementerio de Niembro, en la ensenada de El Vau, en Asturias. “A veces es bonito y, otras, muy bonito”, dice entre risas. “Todo depende de las mareas. Cuando la ría crece, rodea con su caudal las paredes inferiores del cementerio. En ese momento el agua se convierte en un espejo en el que se refleja la iglesia y las tumbas parecen colchonetas sobre las que no hay nadie tumbado”.

Algunos de estos cementerios parecen estar escondidos, como le ocurre al de los ingleses en el monte Urgull de San Sebastián. “Es un jardín de pinos en el que los helechos, el musgo y la maleza, poco a poco, van cubriendo la fosa colectiva, las lápidas y mausoleos de unos militares y oficiales británicos que combatieron en una guerra que no era la suya. La falta de mantenimiento aparente y el silencio, roto por el graznido de las gaviotas, hacen del sitio un lugar misterioso y abandonado”.

Otros, al contrario, son parte del paisaje cotidiano. “En la localidad gallega de Noia es difícil olvidarse del cementerio porque está en medio del pueblo”, explica Martín. “Cuando lo visitas ves a señoras empujando el carro de la compra o a parejas de adolescentes paseando de la mano y protegidos de la lluvia bajo un paraguas. La vida en Noia transcurre entre lápidas y nichos”.

El recorrido de Martín nos lleva a lugares insólitos. En el Cementerio Militar Alemán de Cuacos de Yuste, en Extremadura, descansan los restos de soldados alemanes de la Primera y la Segunda Guerra Mundial que antes estuvieron desperdigados por diferentes cementerios españoles. “Descubrir que hay aviadores, marinos y soldados del ejército de tierra alemán enterrados en un pueblo del norte de Extremadura es como toparse con un buzo colgado de la rama de un árbol en la sierra de Gredos”, dice con humor. En el de Sad Hill, en Burgos, no hay muertos, pero se rodó una de las escenas más míticas del spaghetti western en El bueno, el feo y el malo. Dentro de ese catálogo de rarezas, el libro de Martín también nos lleva a cementerios de mascotas, como el de El Último Parque en Arganda del Rey, o al Museo Mausoleo de Morille, el único de España destinado a enterrar obras de arte.

En tiempos de desmemoria histórica y “truco o trato” made in Hollywood, Martín reivindica la poética de unos lugares que nos conectan con nuestro pasado y, de algún modo, con un futuro ineludible. “Tienen un efecto analgésico y terapéutico, cauterizan heridas”, concluye. A ese respecto, el autor destaca la labor realizada por cementerios como el de Ciriego, en Santander. “Sus actividades ayudan a matizar sus connotaciones negativas y a presentar el cementerio como un lugar mucho más amable. Porque los cementerios hablan, lo que pasa es que no todo el mundo quiere escucharlos. Al fin y al cabo, allí es donde viven los muertos”.

The new report said most of the new NDCs are linked to long-term decarbonisation targets, which involve reaching net zero emissions between 2040 and 2070, with the majority aiming for 2050.  File | Photo Credit: ANI

If countries implement their current climate pledges, global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions are expected to drop only 6% below 2019 levels by 2035, meaning the projected reduction is substantially off track compared to the cut required to limit global warming, a UN report released on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) said.

The ‘2026 Nationally Determined Contributions (NDC) Synthesis Report’, by the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), said that even if these commitments, called NDCs, are fully implemented, including conditional elements, emissions are likely to be just 9% below 2019 levels by 2035.

The report comes days after another UN report revealed that the 1.5°C temperature target was now completely out of reach. It also said the best the world could do was restrict the global rise in temperatures to 1.8°C, and try to pull it back.

The new report said most of the new NDCs are linked to long-term decarbonisation targets, which involve reaching net zero emissions between 2040 and 2070, with the majority aiming for 2050.

Implementation of the NDCs and these long-term targets would imply a best-estimate warming of 1.7°C-2.3°C by the end of the century. “However, returning warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius would require substantial additional GHG emission reductions in the coming years,” the report said.

The findings are based on an examination of 127 new NDCs, representing 154 parties to the 2015 Paris Agreement, submitted between January 1, 2024, and August 31, 2026. Under the Agreement, nations decide their climate actions on their own, and every subsequent set of NDCs must mark a progression over existing ones.

The report said the new generation of NDCs showed climate action was becoming more deeply embedded across economies and societies. “Increasingly, NDCs involve local and regional authorities, civil society and the private sector in planning, implementing and monitoring climate action,” it said. But a lot more is required in terms of cutting GHG emissions to curb global warming.

#878. Pest-Verdacht in Sibirien: Was bisher bekannt ist

Nach dem Tod einer Labormitarbeiterin wächst die Sorge vor der hochansteckenden Lungenpest. Während Russland einen Ausbruch dementiert, fordern internationale Behörden Aufklärung. Was über den Erreger bekannt ist.

Russland stellte am Montag (05.10) klar: Der Tod einer Labormitarbeiterin sei nicht auf einen Pesterreger zurückzuführen. Die 28-Jährige sei an einer "Lungenentzündung unbekannter Herkunft" gestorben, zitiert die russische Nachrichtenagentur Interfax die russische Seuchenbekämpfungsbehörde Rospotrebnadsor.

Demnach seien in Proben der Toten keine Mikroorganismen nachgewiesen worden, "die mit ihrer beruflichen Tätigkeit in Zusammenhang stehen". Damit widerspricht die Behörde bisherigen Informationen.

Lokale Medien hatten zuvor berichtet, dass die Mitarbeiterin eines Instituts zur Bekämpfung von Pesterkrankungen ein Reagenzglas habe fallen lassen. Kurz danach sei sie am vergangenen Freitag im Kreiskrankenhaus der Stadt Schelechow bei Irkutsk in Sibirien gestorben.

Die US-Nachrichtenseite Axios hatte als einer der ersten über den vermeintlichen Vorfall berichtet. Dort wurde ein Mitarbeiter der Trump-Regierung mit den Worten zitiert, man sei sich der Lage bewusst, "beobachte den Ausbruch und prüfe Optionen". Axios hatte auch berichtet, dass rund 200 Menschen unter Beobachtung gestellt wurden, die mit der Verstorbenen in Kontakt gekommen waren. Auch Donald Trump hat sich mittlerweile zu der Situation geäußert und Russland Hilfe angeboten.

Die Weltgesundheitsorganisation (WHO) stuft die Pestgefahr in Irkutsk derzeit als moderat bis niedrig ein , fordert aber Aufklärung. Ähnlich sieht es auch das Europäisches Zentrum für die Prävention und die Kontrolle von Krankheiten ECDC. In einer am 6. Oktober 2026 veröffentlichten Mitteilung erklärte die Organisation jedoch, dass "auf der Grundlage der derzeit nur begrenzt verfügbaren Informationen keine Berichte über Sekundärfälle vorliegen und es keine Hinweise auf eine anhaltende Mensch-zu-Mensch-Übertragung gibt."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Offiziellen russischen Angaben zufolge wurden zwei Krankenhäuser und eine Kinderklinik unter Quarantäne gestellt. Die Mitarbeiterinnen und Mitarbeiter des Instituts befanden sich örtlichen Berichten zufolge an ihrem Arbeitsplatz in Quarantäne. Es habe keine weiteren Infektionen gegeben.

Dennoch herrscht weiter Misstrauen, was die russische Informationspolitik angeht. Auf einem russischsprachigen Social-Media-Kanal der DW schreibt eine Nutzerin:  "Es würde mich nicht wundern, wenn es dort jetzt zu einer Katastrophe kommt, sowohl was die Ausbreitung als auch die Quarantänemaßnahmen angeht." Wie sich die Situation tatsächlich entwickelt, bleibt abzuwarten.

Die Lungenpest ist eine von drei Pestformen - Beulenpest, Pestseptikämie und Lungenpest -, die alle durch dasselbe Bakterium verursacht werden. Das Bakterium nennt sich Yersinia pestis und kommt üblicherweise in Nagetieren vor. Flöhe dienen als sogenannte Vektoren und können das Bakterium dann auf den Menschen übertragen.

Die Weltgesundheitsorganisation (WHO) beschreibt die Lungenpest als die aggressivste Form der Pest. Ihre Inkubationszeit kann bei nur 24 Stunden liegen, und sie ist die einzige Form, die leicht von Mensch zu Mensch übertragen wird. Das geschieht vor alle durch Atemwegspartikel, die beim Husten eines erkrankten Patienten freigesetzt werden. Deshalb könne die Lungenpest schwere Epidemien auslösen.

Die Symptome treten schnell auf: hohes Fieber, Kopfschmerzen und Schwäche, gefolgt von einer sich rasch verschlechternden Lungenentzündung mit Atemnot, Brustschmerzen und einem Husten, der häufig Blut hervorbringt.

Eine Person kann sich mit Lungenpest infizieren, indem sie die Bakterien direkt einatmet, oder die Krankheit entwickelt sich, wenn eine andere Form der Pest, meist die Beulenpest, auf die Lunge übergreift.

Der Unterschied liegt darin, wo sich die Infektion im Körper festsetzt.  Das bestimmt, wie sich die Krankheit ausbreitet und wie tödlich sie ist. Die Beulenpest ist die häufigste Form und jene, bei der die meisten Menschen an den Schwarzen Tod des Mittelalters denken, der etwa 25 Millionen Menschen das Leben gekostet hat.

Sie wird meist durch einen Flohbiss verursacht. Die Bakterien wandern zum nächstgelegenen Lymphknoten, der sich zu einer schmerzhaften Schwellung - einer Beule -  entwickelt. Bleibt die Beulenpest unbehandelt, können sich die Bakterien weiter im Körper ausbreiten. Gelangen sie in den Blutkreislauf, entwickelt sich die Pestseptikämie.

Diese kann Blutungen unter der Haut und Organversagen verursachen. Erreichen die Bakterien die Lunge, entsteht die Lungenpest - die Form, die von Mensch zu Mensch über die Luft übertragen werden kann. Die Pestseptikämie und die Lungenpest können sich auch direkt entwickeln, ohne dass zuvor eine Beule auftritt.

Unbehandelt tötet die Beulenpest laut WHO zwischen 30 und 60 Prozent der Patienten. Die Pestseptikämie und die Lungenpest sind ohne Behandlung immer tödlich.

Die Lungenpest ist heilbar - aber nur, wenn die Behandlung schnell beginnt. Die WHO warnt, dass sie ohne Behandlung innerhalb von 18 bis 24 Stunden nach den ersten Symptomen tödlich enden kann. Gängige Antibiotika können die Infektion heilen, und die Heilungsraten sind hoch, wenn Patienten innerhalb von etwa einem Tag nach Erkrankungsbeginn behandelt werden.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ärzten wird geraten, nicht auf eine Laborbestätigung zu warten, sondern mit der Antibiotikagabe zu beginnen, sobald der Verdacht auf Pest besteht, so die US-amerikanischen Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Die eingesetzten Medikamente sind handelsübliche, weit verbreitete Antibiotika, und Patienten benötigen in der Regel eine Behandlung von bis zu zwei Wochen. Um eine Ausbreitung der Infektion zu verhindern, werden Patienten isoliert. Laut WHO hilft auch das Tragen von Masken.

Personen, die engen Kontakt zu einem Patienten hatten, werden auch behandelt, selbst wenn sie keine Symptome zeigen. Sowohl die WHO als auch die CDC empfehlen für enge Kontaktpersonen von Lungenpest-Erkrankten eine siebentägige vorbeugende Antibiotikabehandlung.

Laut dem Robert-Koch-Institut (RKI) kommt die Pest noch in Ländern Afrikas, Amerikas und Asiens vor. In Deutschland hingegen nicht. Das Risiko der Einreise eines mit dem Pesterreger Infizierten sei gering. Auch gebe es wirksame Maßnahmen, um eine Ausbreitung zu verhindern. Der Artikel wurde am 07.10 aktualisiert.

#879. Albania's student protests are only getting bigger

As police try to suppress anti-corruption protests by young Albanians, Prime Minister Edi Rama is claiming that "antifa" is behind the unrest. Few are buying that explanation.

The fallout from the October 13 protests was still visible when students and faculty from the University of Tirana gathered outside the Education Ministry in Albania's capital on Tuesday to express their continued discontent. Smashed windows have yet to be replaced; the walls are still black with soot from fires that broke out during the protests.

Albania has seen nearly five months of peaceful anti-government protests, sparked initially when plans were made public that Jared Kushner — a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump — and associates intended to build a luxury hotel complex within a nature reserve.

Since then, anti-government and anti-corruption protests have escalated. Now, college and high school students clash with police forces almost daily, with the fiercest clashes so far occurring last week.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Protesters denounce corruption, mismanaged universities and the rising cost of education in Albania — and call for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, who has been in office since 2013.

Wearing a black hooded jacket and a scarf across her face to conceal her identity, a woman who asked to be called Sara because she fears repercussions for speaking to the press told DW that protesters "communicate via text messages — that's the only way."

She cut the interview short as some protesters began flinging stones at the Education Ministry. Police pushed demonstrators and journalists out of the way, using water cannons to disperse the crowd.

"Social media is the most important public space today — more so than physical spaces," Besmir Semanaj, a prominent Albanian cybersecurity advocate told DW. "Young Albanians no longer organize through traditional structures such as political parties, associations or public appeals. Instead, they organize themselves where they spend much of their daily lives: on their cellphones."

"The most important communication channels include Instagram, WhatsApp groups for academic-year cohorts, departments and dormitories, Telegram channels for general announcements, and TikTok for sharing videos," Semanaj said. He added that people who are especially concerned with security use the Signal messaging app.

"This is a horizontal organizational structure, without individual 'leaders' and without a central command structure," Semanaj said. "That is exactly why the government is having such a hard time understanding and controlling the situation."

Semanaj said the Telegram messenger app had proven particularly useful for protesters. "Telegram channels allow you to reach tens of thousands of people at once," he said. "Notifications are sent out within seconds, and external control is more difficult to establish than on traditional platforms."

Rama has called the youth uprising a "hybrid war." He said protesters thought they could "make Albania a better country through TikTok and without even being able to string together more than seven coherent words." Though not all are terrorists, he said, he believes that "they are hostages to a certain mindset, a new ideology that has only one goal: to destroy, to turn everything upside down, to raze everything to the ground."

Over nearly five months, Rama has accused various "true" masterminds of organizing the anti-government and anti-corruption protests. He has alleged that the governments of Greece, Russia and Iran are stirring up dissent.

Most recently, Rama said it was "antifa" — or a decentralized movement of global antifascists — that had stoked anti-government and anti-corruption sentiments in Albania. "These are young people who have been radicalized and ideologically indoctrinated and who are acting under the pressure or influence of a new, dark force that has emerged in Europe and the United States, a force that the President of the United States has designated as a terrorist organization: Antifa," Rama claimed.

Redion Qirjazi, a security affairs researcher who focuses on violence prevention and conflict resolution, told DW that Rama's claim was not likely to prove true. "That is a serious accusation — one that requires equally compelling evidence," Qirjazi said. "To date, no verifiable evidence has been presented to prove the existence of an organized Antifa structure in Albania, let alone its involvement in coordinating the protests."

Qirjazi said Rama's reference to Trump's calling antifa a terror group was problematic. "Antifa is not a unified international organization with a centralized structure or leadership," he said, "but rather an umbrella term for various movements and groups united by the fact that they are, at their core, anti-fascist."

Sara said she rejected the "terrorist" label that Rama had attempted to slap on her and her fellow protesters. "There are groups that are willing to use violence — that's true — but I have nothing to do with them," she said. "As soon as I see violence, I walk away; I'm against it."

Arlind Qori, the chairman of the Together Movement, a social-democratic opposition party with just one seat in Albania's parliament, said youths had taken to the streets out of dissatisfaction with the status quo rather than any particular ideology. "Young Albanians are outraged by the current socioeconomic conditions: the poverty, the fact that many of their parents have emigrated because they couldn't support their families, the decline of the education system, the lack of postgraduation prospects," Qori said. The students' central demand is for Rama to resign, he added  "not a socialist revolution."

"People aren't demanding anything radical," Qori said. "They merely want a corrupt head of government to resign — that's a fundamental and moderate demand. But Edi Rama continues to meet this demand with police violence and arrogance."

Qirjazi said Rama's allegations of foreign interference could be a strategy. "When a government faces protests and public discontent, linking demonstrators to extremism and foreign influence may serve to divert attention away from the actual causes and toward a national security narrative," he said.

"This can serve several political purposes: to delegitimize the protesters, to weaken their support among the public, and to justify a tougher crackdown in the name of law and order," Qirjazi said.

Semanaj said this was a common pattern in governments' efforts to dismiss dissent. "Protests are portrayed as acts of violence," he said. "Young people are cast as manipulated, and their legitimate concerns — conditions at universities, tuition fees, corruption and a lack of prospects — vanish from the news agenda."

#880. ‘Los cuatro pasaron el día juntos’, de Chris Kraus: un crimen real, un mundo enfermo

La escritora estadounidense ofrece un libro inclasificable donde la autoficción y la crítica social se entrelazan con la historia verdadera del asesinato de un joven a manos de un amigo

Termino la lectura de la nueva novela de la estadounidense Chris Kraus, Los cuatro pasaron el día juntos (Random House, 2026) y me quedo con más dudas que certezas en cuanto a su factura literaria, pero con la agobiante sensación de haber visitado un mundo que padece de enfermedades que podrían ser terminales.

Comparada con la Premio Nobel francesa Annie Ernaux por el uso de la llamada autoficción, Chris Kraus escogió como uno de los asuntos para armar este libro difícilmente clasificable la historia de un crimen real ocurrido en una pequeña población de Minnesota, Estados Unidos, en 2019. Uno de esos cuatro jóvenes “que habían pasado el día juntos” bebiendo y drogándose, mató a otro de dos disparos en la cara porque, supuestamente, el asesinado se había propasado con su novia, otra de los jóvenes encartados en el suceso. Sin embargo, esta historia real y documentada solo ocupa la tercera parte y final de la obra, titulada ‘Harding’, mientras las dos primeras se centran (¿novelescamente?), una en la familia de la niña Catherine en los años que viven en Milford, Connecticut, y la otra en la cincuentona Catt, como en su adolescencia decidió llamarse aquella niña que fue Catherine, ahora convertida en escritora y crítica de arte radicada en la gélida población de Balsam, Minnesota, que le da nombre a este sector del libro.

La primera parte está enfocada en la vida de Jasper y Emma, padres de Catherine y luego de Carla y corre hasta el momento en que, por cuestiones laborales, toda la familia se traslada a Nueva Zelanda (y prácticamente desaparecen del relato). Frecuentes cambios de domicilio y pérdidas de puestos de trabajo, diversas relaciones y conflictos familiares que incluyen la posible discapacidad mental de la hermana pequeña Carla, traban el desarrollo dramático de la historia que llega a resultar tan farragoso que por momentos da la impresión de no saber adónde va o adónde pretendía llegar el argumento. Pero aun así en su tránsito deja, y esta es quizás la esencia perseguida, una imagen no demasiado amable de la vida de la clase trabajadora estadounidense en los años que corren desde la década de 1930 hasta la de 1950, una época mitificada como la del paraíso de la clase media.

En el segundo tercio, ‘Balsam’, la historia se concentra en Catt sin que se hagan muchas referencias a su pasado mediato. Poco se nos dirá de su vida en Nueva Zelanda e, incluso, del destino de sus padres y, sobre todo, de la hermana Carla, al parecer (digo al parecer) víctima de algún tipo de autismo ya advertido en el primer tramo. Ahora Catt, escritora de cierto éxito, divorciada de un generoso anciano francés y casada con Paul García, un hombre diez años más joven al cual ella ha intentado redimir de una juventud turbia que lo llevó a la cárcel. Pero Paul, que gracias a Catt llega a tener un título como psicólogo, resulta ser un adicto insalvable: su alcoholismo crónico se convierte en un constante ir y venir de la dependencia a la sobriedad (casi siempre por obligación legal, más que por decisión personal) para volver a la dependencia. Una y otra vez, por años, una y otra vez reflejado en el libro. El resultado es que este sector termina por armar la crónica de una relación sentimental dolorosa y Catt solo encuentra un alivio en sus trabajos literarios y sus contactos con la dura naturaleza de la región, mientras se pregunta si haber intentado la redención de Paul solo fue una quimera.

Entonces, mientras se vive uno de los momentos críticos de la vida de la pareja y del país con el inicio del primer mandato de Donald Trump (al que la autora machaca sin piedad), se produce otro acontecimiento que perturba más aún la vida de Catt cuando es “cancelada” por determinadas opiniones genéricas y acciones económicas (la renta de unos apartamentos). Viviendo esta crisis profesional y existencial, la escritora Catt conoce del tremebundo crimen de Harding, un suceso en el que se vieron envueltos esos “cuatro que pasaron el día juntos”, de los cuales tres son poco más que adolescentes. Y Chris Kraus le da un timonazo a la narración.

Desde las dos primeras partes del libro, quizás el tramo más novelesco del volumen, la autora va dando testimonios de los males que corroen a su entorno social. Como si fuera la realidad más palpable de su mundo, desfilan por estas páginas abundantes historias de niños con vida rotas, abandonados por sus padres, internados en reformatorios o acogidos por otras familias; niños y adultos con enfermedades mentales o sicológicas, como cierto personaje mencionado que llegó a albergar 15 personalidades diferentes, entre otros fenómenos; un mundo plagado de alcohólicos y drogadictos de todo tipo, consumidores (incluso desde la niñez) de los más disímiles estupefacientes, como es el caso de los encartados en el crimen de Harding, adictos al cristal y la metanfetamina, entre otras sustancias que hace parecer a la marihuana algo tan normal como ingerir una aspirina; una sociedad, en fin, en la que junto a estas conductas sociales (o gracias a ellas) prosperan los fundamentalismos económicos, religiosos, políticos, sociales, raciales, un universo en donde el odio se impone al diálogo y la comprensión.

Lo que en una época de oro de la novelística estadounidense muchas veces se presentó como un retrato posible de una sociedad afectada por la alienación y dio, entre otras, obras como las de J. D. Salinger o John Updike, o que se dedicó a indagar en los conflictos sociales, como lo hicieron, siempre entre otros, Philip Roth y James Baldwin, ahora nos ofrece a una Chris Kraus que hunde las manos en el aceite hirviente de una sociedad que parece devorarse a sí misma por sus cada vez más altos niveles de alienación e inconformidad social, unas crisis económicas y existenciales que han tenido a la figura del presidente Donald Trump y sus comportamientos y decisiones como una especie de catalizador muy capaz de acelerar el proceso. Quizás esta mirada corrosiva de su tiempo sea la mayor virtud de este libro de Chris Kraus, inclasificable y lleno de padecimientos humanos y sociales.

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla and Vice-President of Cuba’s National Assembly of People’s Power and the Council of State, Ana Maria Mari Machado pose for a group photograph with other delegates during their meeting ahead of the 12th BRICS Parliamentary Forum 2026, in New Delhi on Sunday, October 25, 2026. Photo credit: X/@loksabhaspeaker via ANI

Ahead of Cuba’s resolution against the U.S. blockade to be taken up by the UN General Assembly on October 27, the Caribbean nation intensified its diplomatic outreach to the Global South on Sunday (October 25, 2026), with the Vice President of Cuba’s National Assembly of People’s Power and the Council of State Mari Machado meeting Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla here.

Following the meeting with Ms. Machado, Mr. Birla said they had “discussed strengthening parliamentary exchanges, capacity-building and cooperation in healthcare and pharmaceuticals.” Cuba is  participating in the BRICS Parliamentary Forum meeting as a partner country of the grouping.

This comes two days after Cuba’s ambassador to India Juan Carlos Marsan Aguilera accused the United States of carrying out a naval blockade that has created an acute energy crisis in his country. “Cuba is fully capable of defending itself. The U.S. is practising the Monroe Doctrine in our region,” Mr. Aguilera said, seeking support for Cuba’s UNGA resolution.

Also Read: BRICS Forum adopts joint declaration; condemns Pahalgam attack, seeks UNSC reforms

Mr. Birla also met the Chairman of the State Duma of Russia, Vyacheslav Volodin, on Saturday (October 24), to discuss bilateral ties. India and Russia are marking the 80th anniversary of their bilateral relationship and the two dignitaries carried out a review of parliament-level exchanges between the two countries against the backdrop of unfolding global and regional developments.

The Lok Sabha Speaker informed the Russian delegation about the steps taken to make parliamentary proceedings accessible in various Indian languages through Sansad Bhashini. According to a statement issued by the Parliament Secretariat, Mr. Birla highlighted the importance of using technology in making parliamentary functioning more accessible, efficient, and people-centric.

#885. Hong Kong beautician gets 4 years for selling friends to Myanmar scam hub

Judge slams defendant’s actions as ‘vicious and inhumane’ after victims were trafficked to infamous ‘KK Park’ compound and held for US$500,000 ransom

A Hong Kong beautician has been sentenced to four years in jail for tricking two friends into forced labour and confinement in Myanmar’s notorious “KK Park” scam farm, with a judge slamming her actions as “vicious and inhumane”.

District Court Judge Adriana Noelle Tse Ching on Tuesday said the 33-year-old defendant, Poon Sum-yi, had premeditated the fraudulent scheme to lure the two victims into travelling to Thailand, before selling them to the Chinese-run scam compound in neighbouring Myanmar for US$54,000 in December 2024.

The two victims – unemployed Peng Xinying and part-time model Liu Bingbing – were Poon’s friends and were initially invited by her to join her on a trip to Japan or Canada.

#887. Are the French police the most violent in the EU?

As protests continue in France, the French police are under scrutiny after new allegations of police brutality. The force has a bigger arsenal than most in Europe.

Videos of alleged police violence are going viral on French social media as a wave of protests grips France. One video shows the police beating a man to the floor then dragging him away unconscious. Another shows an officer grabbing a young man from behind, seemingly unprovoked, and dragging him by the neck. Another shows a young woman being hauled off with a twisted arm, screaming in pain. These videos could not be independently verified.

The French police have drawn renewed criticism from rights groups, not only because of their methods but also because of their use of stun grenades and rubber bullets. France has one of the most heavily armed police forces in Europe. During the student protests of the past weeks, several teenagers sustained life-changing injuries as a result: One had a hand blown off, one was blinded in one eye, another had his jaw broken.

More than half a million people took to the streets in France on Saturday, most of whom protested peacefully, criticizing public sector cuts, the cost-of-living crisis and supporting students' demands for better conditions in classrooms.

Rioters took advantage, burning buildings, looting stores and lobbing projectiles at the police, creating a difficult situation for the officers and other emergency services.

The protests over the weekend followed a series of protests by high-school students, who barricaded school buildings to denounce a shortage of teachers and demand repairs to crumbling infrastructure.

More protests will be happening this weekend, with the French government saying it will even deploy military forces.

The French police have a bigger arsenal than most European countries. For instance, officers use the so-called LBD-40, a type of gun used to fire rubber bullets.

Many countries, like the UK and Germany, mostly do not allow the use of rubber bullets in protests.  In some European countries, like Spain, they are sometimes used but cause fewer injuries than in France.

"It is not a French specificity. But there are guidelines. There must be a certain distance," Anastassia Tsoukala, an associate professor of criminology at the University of Paris-Sud, told DW. "Even if you try to respect the guidelines, people may move and then all of a sudden they may lose one eye. So it's extremely dangerous."

Police in France routinely use tear gas, as do police in many other countries in Europe. In warfare, its use is actually forbidden under agreements like the Chemical Weapons Convention.

What makes the French police stand out from other forces is its use of stun grenades.

"These grenades contain a high level of explosive substances. So from this point of view, France is unique," said Tsoukala.

Minister of the Interior Laurent Nunez insists that weapons used by the police are "non-lethal." However, some of the equipment used by the force is classified by France's own internal security code as "war material."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The police's use of these weapons has received renewed criticism after it resulted in injuries during the protests. The teenager who lost use of an eye is suspected of being hit at close range with a rubber bullet from an LBD-40.

"When we look at crowd control, it is clear that if we measure police brutality by the number of deaths amongst demonstrators or members of the crowd, and if we also measure it by the number of cases of maiming, the French police are the most brutal in the whole of the European Union," says Sebastian Roche, a researcher at France's National Centre for Scientific Research who specializes in comparing police forces across Europe.

He points to the political context to understand the French police's equipment and how it is used today.

"The political authorities are free to decide on the police's equipment," the police expert says. "When LBDs were introduced into the [French] police force, they were intended for units like anti-organized crime units. This is the same weapon that is today used for crowd control. It gives an idea of how the way in which politicians in France think we can or should deal with political protest has evolved."

Another difference between the French police and forces elsewhere is the methods. German police, for example, are supposed to try to avoid escalation.

Roche compares how protestors were moved in Lützerath, Germany, in 2023 to the more aggressive methods in Sainte-Soline, France, in 2023. Both places saw environmental protests.

"In Lützerath, dogs were used, there were some injuries but far fewer seriously injured people on both sides. In Sainte-Soline, the military police was sent in and used LBDs and grenades intensively. There were serious injuries amongst both police officers and demonstrators. Two protestors were left in a coma."

According to international standards set by the United Nations, use of force by officers of the law "should be exceptional," in the case of "prevention of crime" or "lawful arrest." Any use of force should follow a principle of "proportionality," which means no more than necessary to achieve its objective.

French Interior Minister Nunez has insisted in radio interviews that officers have largely respected this principle, which is also enshrined in French law, during the current protests.

However, rights group Amnesty International describes the police response to the current protests as "disproportionate" and calls upon French authorities to "act upon their human rights obligations."

The French branch of the League of Human Rights condemns the "violent repression" of the high school protest movement.

DW contacted two police unions and the French Interior Ministry for comment, but none responded before time of publication.

"It was very complicated to contain all the different groups," Interior Minister Nunez said in Marseille on Tuesday. "The police did a great job and there were a great number of crimes that were prevented thanks to their commitment."

Experts are critical of the police's actions.

"Public order is subordinated to human life and safety," Tsoukala said. "As a jurist I should say that this is a non-negotiable value."

The French police have no independent watchdog, only an internal division called the IGPN (General Inspectorate of the National Police) that can investigate when problems occur. The IGPN says it has opened at least 40 cases since the beginning of the latest protests.

Countries like the UK and Denmark investigate incidents differently, with independent watchdogs. However, Tsoukala criticizes leniency and a lack of transparency across Europe when incidents with the police occur.

"They are acquitted or they receive extremely light penalties," she said. "And I'm afraid this is the standard method to deal with police brutality cases across Europe."

Updated - October 27, 2026 04:33 pm IST - Nairobi

A health worker dressed in Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) in a room at an Ebola isolation facility at The Nairobi Hospital, Kenya. | Photo Credit: AP

Kenya's Health Ministry announced the country's second Ebola death on Friday (October 23, 2026), saying a 65-year-old woman who was a close relative of the first patient died after developing symptoms while in quarantine.

The woman began showing symptoms 10 days ago and began receiving supportive care at an infectious disease unit in the capital, Nairobi.

The Ministry said medical personnel "did everything possible to save her life", but she died on Friday (October 23) evening.

Her family was notified, and the Ministry said it would arrange a safe and dignified burial in consultation with relatives.

Also Read: Congo’s Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as authorities race to slow spread in African countries

The remaining seven Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities. No new infections were reported.

Kenya announced its first ever Ebola case on October 6 after a 40-year-old Kenyan man who was living in Congo travelled to Kenya via Uganda, arriving on October 3. He was driven by a relative to Nairobi Hospital, where he tested positive for Ebola on October 5 and died the same day.

Authorities have identified some 135 contacts of the first patient, placing 118 in quarantine. Eight tested positive while in quarantine, including four health workers and four close family members.

The Health Ministry said some contacts who completed the 21-day quarantine period without developing symptoms would be released starting Saturday (October 24).

In Nigeria, authorities said on Friday (October 23) that they were yet to verify how the country's first Ebola patient contracted the disease. The woman tested positive for the virus upon her return to Nigeria's capital of Abuja from Uganda.

The woman — married to a Swiss diplomat in Nigeria whom she had been travelling with — did not visit Congo and "is believed to have contracted the virus whilst travelling to Uganda", Switzerland's Federal Department of Foreign Affairs, or FDFA, told The Associated Press on Friday (October 23).

Her husband has not shown any symptoms and remains in isolation, the FDFA added.

Nigeria's Health Minister Muhammad Pate told reporters on Friday (October 23) that the Nigerian patient "appears to be closely related" to the first case in Kenya in terms of the nature of their infection. "That may or may not change the understanding of the route of transmission given that the virus itself takes time to change," Mr. Pate said.

The Africa CDC earlier said the first patients in Nigeria and Kenya had travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport on October 3.

United States health officials this week said that all passengers boarding an international flight to the U.S. — no matter from where — must sign a statement attesting that they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. The US has been screening travellers from Ebola-affected countries during the current outbreak.

Travellers who were in Congo in the three weeks leading to their trip will not be allowed to board flights with U.S. destinations, including Americans, the U.S. CDC said on Thursday (October 22).

Ebola is highly contagious and spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person, including blood and vomit, or through contact with contaminated materials and surfaces, such as bedding and clothing. Congo is experiencing its deadliest outbreak, with at least 4,000 deaths since May.

#891. Chemie-Nobelpreis geht an Forscher aus Frankreich und Japan

Der Chemie-Nobelpreis würdigt in diesem Jahr zwei Forscher für grundlegende Entdeckungen zur Entstehung asymmetrischer Moleküle. Ihre Arbeit ist auch für die Entwicklung von Arzneimitteln wichtig.

Der Franzose Henri Kagan und der Japaner Kenso Soai werden mit dem Nobelpreis für Chemie ausgezeichnet für die Entdeckung nichtlinearer Effekte und der Autokatalyse in der asymmetrischen organischen Synthese. Das gab die Königlich-Schwedische Akademie der Wissenschaften in Stockholm bekannt.

Ihre Forschung half dabei, ein lange bestehendes Rätsel der Chemie zu lösen. Viele Moleküle, darunter Aminosäuren, können in zwei Varianten vorkommen. Diese verhalten sich zueinander wie Bild und Spiegelbild. In lebenden Organismen findet sich jedoch jeweils nur eine dieser Formen. Lange war unklar, wie eine solche chemische Asymmetrie entstehen kann.

Kagan von der Université Paris-Sud und Soai von der Tokyo University of Science lieferten mit ihren Arbeiten wichtige Erklärungen dafür. Nach Angaben der Nobel-Akademie waren ihre Entdeckungen entscheidend für Chemiker, die Grundlagen für die Herstellung von Arzneimitteln entwickeln.

Der Chemie-Nobelpreis gilt als renommierteste Auszeichnung des Fachs. In diesem Jahr ist er mit insgesamt zwölf Millionen schwedischen Kronen dotiert, umgerechnet rund einer Million Euro.

Die Nobelstiftung hatte das Preisgeld anlässlich des 125-jährigen Bestehens der Nobelpreise um eine Million Kronen erhöht. "In diesem Jahr feiern wir das 125-jährige Bestehen des Nobelpreises. Aus diesem Anlass freuen wir uns, das Preisgeld um eine Million erhöhen zu können", sagte die Geschäftsführerin der Nobelstiftung, Hanna Stjärne.

Auch bei der Bekanntgabe gibt es im Jubiläumsjahr eine Premiere. Erstmals werden die Namen der Nobelpreisträger für Physik, Chemie und Wirtschaftswissenschaften von einer Frau verkündet.

Ellen Moons ist seit Anfang 2026 Generalsekretärin der Königlich-Schwedischen Akademie der Wissenschaften. Die gebürtige Belgierin ist die erste Frau auf diesem Posten seit Gründung der Akademie im Jahr 1739.

Im vergangenen Jahr hatten Susumu Kitagawa, Richard Robson und Omar Yaghi den Chemie-Nobelpreis erhalten. Sie wurden für die Entwicklung metallorganischer Gerüstverbindungen ausgezeichnet. Die Strukturen können unter anderem Wasser aus Wüstenluft gewinnen, Kohlendioxid abscheiden oder chemische Reaktionen katalysieren.

Seit 1901 wurde der Chemie-Nobelpreis an 198 verschiedene Forscher vergeben. Zwei von ihnen erhielten die Auszeichnung zweimal. Unter den Geehrten waren bislang acht Frauen. Dazu gehören Marie Curie, die 1911 ausgezeichnet wurde, sowie Emmanuelle Charpentier und Jennifer Doudna. Sie erhielten den Preis 2020 für die Entwicklung einer Genschere.

Die diesjährige Nobelpreis-Woche hatte am Montag mit der Medizin begonnen. Ausgezeichnet werden die Deutschen Peter Hegemann und Georg Nagel sowie der US-Forscher Karl Deisseroth für ihre Entdeckungen in der Optogenetik. Mit dieser Methode lassen sich Zellen mithilfe von Licht gezielt an- und abschalten.

Am Dienstag wurde der Physik-Nobelpreis dem belgisch-amerikanischen Forscher Francis Halzen zugesprochen. Gewürdigt wurden seine Beiträge zum Neutrino-Observatorium "IceCube" in der Antarktis, mit dem erstmals hochenergetische kosmische Neutrinos nachgewiesen wurden.

Am Donnerstag und Freitag werden die Nobelpreise für Literatur und Frieden bekanntgegeben. Am kommenden Montag folgt der von der schwedischen Reichsbank gestiftete Wirtschaftspreis.

Die Auszeichnungen werden traditionell am 10. Dezember überreicht, dem Todestag des Preisstifters Alfred Nobel.

#892. El Real Madrid es un relámpago: 14 segundos por posesión y 15 triples por partido

El conjunto de Pedro Martínez bate récords en las cinco primeras jornadas de la ACB con 112,8 puntos por encuentro

Nadie ataca tan rápido y tira con tanta efectividad de tres puntos como el Real Madrid, un torbellino en la Liga Endesa. Son cinco victorias consecutivas, líder en solitario por delante de La Laguna Tenerife, y 112,8 puntos de media por encuentro, récord histórico de la competición. El método que el técnico Pedro Martínez ha importado desde el Valencia Basket ha casado con unos jugadores rápidos y muy afilados en el tiro y el resultado es un equipo por ahora arrollador.

La revolución del Madrid se explica por su capacidad para fusionar con éxito dos factores: velocidad y acierto. Uno no sirve sin el otro en la pizarra de Pedro Martínez y los peones blancos han asimilado la idea hasta ponerla en práctica sobre la cancha de la mejor manera. Las cifras avalan los dos vectores. El Madrid luce las posesiones más cortas de la liga, 14 segundos de media, por delante del Breogán (14,1s), consume una tercera parte de sus ataques en los 10 primeros segundos y es el conjunto con menos posesiones finalizadas entre los segundos 21 y 24, apenas un 15,5% (le sigue el colista Manresa con un 16,2%).

Esa velocidad para correr y lanzar se une en la ecuación del éxito al uso masivo de los tiros de tres puntos y a unos altos porcentajes de acierto. El Madrid corre, lanza de tres y anota. Ese ha sido su mecanismo más habitual y así ha despellejado a sus rivales. En los últimos tres partidos en ocho días entre el torneo casero y la Euroliga, los hombres de Pedro Martínez han enchufado 65 triples: 20 de 42 intentos (48% de acierto) ante el Surne Bilbao en la victoria por 119-84, entonces récord triplista blanco en un encuentro liguero; 21 de 40 lanzamientos ante el Maccabi (52% y triunfo por 99-113), su mejor registro en Europa; y 24 de 45 (53% y 86-122) al Ilerna Lleida, la mejor marca vista nunca en la ACB.

En esos tres encuentros que resumen su explosión anotadora tiró el Madrid muchas más veces de tres puntos que de dos. La cita de este domingo pasado contra el conjunto catalán la remató el equipo de Pedro Martínez con 41 puntos solo en el último cuarto (10 triples en ese periodo) y los franceses Maledon (siete de ocho en triples, incluido uno en el último segundo del partido) y Luwawu-Cabarrot (siete de nueve) en estado de gracia. A ellos se unen Campazzo y Andrés Feliz para componer una línea exterior demoledora. Son ya 75 triples convertidos en cinco partidos ligueros (15 por jornada), por los 63 del Río Breogán y el Surne Bilbao (12,6), los siguientes en este listado.

“Ahora mismo la tendencia que hay clarísimamente en la ACB y también en Europa es de posesiones cortas, buscar la ventaja rápido y jugar con una intensidad alta. En la liga española llevamos varias temporadas jugando a ese nivel y esa tendencia se está sumando cada vez más a Europa. Es un tipo de baloncesto con el que yo me siento a gusto, pero no hay una manera única de jugar bien. Es una corriente que ya veremos lo que dura porque los equipos que no quieran jugar a ese ritmo se adaptarán y harán cosas para evitarlo”, explicaba a este periódico Pedro Martínez.

El técnico, de 65 años, convirtió al Valencia Basket en campeón liguero el año pasado y en el líder de la ACB en valoración, puntos, rebotes, asistencias y triples convertidos, exactamente las mismas estadísticas que ahora encabeza el Real Madrid, además de tapones y faltas recibidas. El entrenador ha sometido a sus jugadores a un curso acelerado de un método que incluye también las rotaciones constantes y los cambios múltiples, un nuevo sistema de juego que ya le ha coronado como vencedor de la Supercopa de la Euroliga frente al Olympiacos. En la competición europea ha revertido con cuatro victorias seguidas las tres derrotas iniciales, todas como visitante y por marcadores ajustados, y en la ACB manda con puño de hierro. El Madrid es un relámpago que vuela de tres en tres.

#897. Ukraine: Life near the front line in Sloviansk

As Russian continues to attack Sloviansk in eastern Ukraine, thousands of residents refuse to leave or struggle to find a way out. For many, poverty, family ties and beloved pets make evacuation painfully difficult.

A few days ago, three Russian aerial bombs struck a residential neighborhood on the outskirts of Sloviansk. One hit a five-story apartment building, injuring seven people. Along with neighboring Kramatorsk, Sloviansk is one of the last major towns in the eastern Ukrainian region of Donetsk still under Ukrainian control. Since summer, the city has been a combat zone.

In a courtyard surrounded by damaged apartment blocks, a dusty carpet hangs over the metal frame of a swing set. Tetjana, a pensioner who lives in the building across the street, has brought it out of her rubble-strewn apartment to clean it. She was in her kitchen when the bombs struck.

"The bomb hit the second floor, and a woman who lived on the fourth floor was screaming," she tells DW. "They managed to rescue her before that entire section of the building collapsed," she adds.

Despite being offered the opportunity to evacuate, Tetjana has yet to leave Sloviansk. "I don't know where I would go," she says. Rent can cost up to €400 ($449) a month. Tetjana's pension is the equivalent of just €67 ($75) a month. Even with monthly relocation assistance of about €40 ($45), she could not make ends meet. "I couldn't live on that. Nowhere!"

Meanwhile, electricity and water are still available in her neighborhood, but the gas supply has been cut off. "We'll get through this," Tetjana says hopefully. "Everything will be OK. That's what I tell everyone. I want that so much."

Days after the attack, the few residents remaining in the damaged buildings were still clearing out their apartments. But another attack hit as they worked. This time, the bombs struck a building housing a state-run emergency assistance center and the Red Cross. While firefighters put out the blaze, rescue workers and volunteers retrieved belongings left inside and cleared away broken glass. Eight people were injured in the attack.

"I was on the balcony when there was a deafening bang. It felt as if someone had hit me over the head," says Natalja, describing one of the recent attacks. The pensioner comes to this part of the city to care for her twin sister. "She can no longer get around. Today, I couldn't bring her bread, only crispbread," she tells DW. Although shops and a few stalls remain at the burned-out market, bread is not available every day.

"I tried to persuade my sister to leave. I would go to a nursing home and she would go to a hospital. But her dog is sick, and I have one, too," Natalja says, noting that pets are not allowed during evacuations. "I can't leave my sister behind. She is worried and angry with me, as if everything were my fault. I have no strength left."

Natalja slowly sets off for home, "so I can get there before dark." The city center is nearly 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) away. Public transportation has been suspended since 30 people were killed in an attack on two buses in neighboring Kramatorsk.

The center of Sloviansk is heavily damaged. Few people are out on the streets, though a handful of shops remain open. Of the city's 100,000 residents, about 20,000 remain, most of them elderly people who are unable to leave.

Vasyl, a pensioner, is from the village of Mayaky, north of Sloviansk. A neighbor drove him into the city center, where he sat down for lunch in a cafe. "We're used to living under fire by now," he says. "But it's a bad habit. We should have broken it long ago."

Vasyl wants peace for his homeland. But he rejects Russian President Vladimir Putin's demand that the part of the Donetsk region under Ukrainian control be handed over to Moscow.

Two elderly women talk on a street covered with nets to protect against drones. "I can't remember the last time I slept through the night," says Iryna, a pensioner. "It's terrible, but I have nowhere to go. I'm supposed to leave my two cats behind, but I love them so much. They're all I have."

"We can only hide, trembling, and pray to God that everything will be all right," Iryna continues. "When I have to go to the market, I don't know if I'll make it there alive."

Russian drones attacked the central market several weeks ago, injuring at least three people. Since then, fewer vendors and customers have been coming to the market.

Valeriya sells women's underwear. With kindergartens closed, she has to bring her 5-year-old daughter Sofia to work. Their neighborhood in Sloviansk is not yet subject to the mandatory evacuation of families with children.

"We're used to this life by now. We were evacuated in 2022, but later returned. Now we're waiting to be evacuated again," Valeriya says.

Sofia races through the market aisles with her friend Anya, who is a year older. Anya's mother is a soldier defending her hometown. Her grandmother, Tetjana, sits nearby selling men's clothing. She, too, has to look after her granddaughter while working.

Tetjana has started shipping her belongings to the Dnipropetrovsk region, where she hopes to start a new life. She is sending them while the post office is still open. "It hurts to see our Ukraine being destroyed," she says, fighting back tears. "Who will rebuild our cities?"

She hopes to return one day. But the fate of Bakhmut weighs on her mind. "Look at Bakhmut. There are no houses left. I'm counting on our boys to hold our cities, even though it's very difficult." Bakhmut, about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from Sloviansk, fell to Russian forces in 2023 after months of heavy fighting.

The women see little hope for a ceasefire. "Putin won't want one. And our younger generation will ask us what we fought for in the first place," Tetjana says. She believes Russia must withdraw from Ukrainian territory.

Drones buzz overhead as gunfire echoes across the market. "It's hard for our boys to shoot them down," Tetjana says. "But they're doing their best."

A B1 bomber prepares to take off as police officers guard a checkpoint near RAF Fairford air base, in Fairford, England, on September 29, 2026. | Photo Credit: AP

Two men were charged on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) with national security offences over a suspected plot against RAF Fairford, a U.S.-run military air base in England, police and prosecutors said.

British-Iranian dual national Mohmed Abdulkarim and British citizen Nouman Essghir, both aged 24 and from London, were charged under the National Security Act, the Crown Prosecution Service said. They are due to appear in court later on Tuesday (October 27, 2026).

Also Read | U.S. Air Force removes all bombers from British air base targeted by a suspected terror attack

Abdulkarim is charged with assisting Iran’s intelligence service and Essghir with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the U.K.

RAF Fairford, in western England, has been used by American bombers to strike Iran during this year’s war.

Essghir was arrested outside the base on September 27, when armed police officers and Army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area. Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes as police and army bomb-disposal experts searched for explosives.

Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant — gasoline — in vans at the scene, but no explosives.

Also Read | U.K. PM Burnham says Iran’s IRGC likely behind RAF Fairford incident

Essghir was initially released on bail before being re-arrested last week. Abdulkarim was arrested in the past week. Six other men have been arrested and released on bail as investigations continue.

British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which led the U.S. to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that the apparent plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard.

Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

Also Read | U.K. police arrest five for preparing ‘terrorist act’ as incident near air base probed

Earlier this month, the head of Britain’s MI5 spy agency warned that both Iran and Russia were expanding their attacks against the U.K., and that the RAF Fairford incident was not unique.

Ken McCallum, who leads the U.K.’s domestic security service, said Tehran is seeking to intensify its attacks in Britain beyond the traditional targets of Iranians opposed to the country’s Islamic authorities. He said more than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year.

“We have seen a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state, and as the director general of MI5 said just the other week, we are working together to intervene, identify and respond to that threat,” said Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, the head of National Counter Terrorism Policing in the U.K.
